question: Compare the quantitative triggers in the four-leg All-Way Stop crash warrant and the 8-hour volume warrant.
model_answer: Direct Answer: The two all-way stop warrants use different metrics: the crash warrant is triggered by crash frequency, while the 8-hour volume warrant is triggered by multimodal entering volumes. For a four-leg intersection, the crash warrant is met by five or more reported crashes in 12 months or six or more in 36 months (of a type correctable by all-way stop control), whereas the 8-hour volume warrant requires at least 300 combined vehicle/bicycle/pedestrian units per hour from the major-street approaches and at least 200 units per hour from the minor-street approaches for each of the same 8 hours of a typical day. Both are Option (permissive) provisions, so meeting either threshold permits — but does not require — all-way stop control based on an engineering study. Options (permitted): - Crash warrant (four-leg trigger): "All-way stop control may be installed at an intersection where an engineering study indicates that: A. For a four-leg intersection, there are five or more reported crashes in a 12-month period or six or more reported crashes in a 36-month period that were of a type susceptible to correction by the installation of all-way stop control." - 8-hour volume warrant: "All-way stop control may be installed at an intersection where an engineering study indicates: A. The combined motor vehicle, bicycle, and pedestrian volume entering the intersection from the major-street approaches is at least 300 units per hour for each of any 8 hours of a typical day; and B. The combined motor vehicle, bicycle, and pedestrian volume entering the intersection from the minor-street approaches is at least 200 units per hour for each of any of the same 8 hours." - Key contrasts: (1) metric — crash counts (5/yr or 6/3 yr, four legs) versus hourly volumes (300 major / 200 minor units per hour); (2) time frame — 12- or 36-month crash history versus any 8 hours of a single typical day; (3) mode coverage — the volume warrant explicitly combines motor vehicles, bicycles, and pedestrians, while the crash warrant counts reported crashes of a correctable type; (4) the volume warrant's two thresholds must both be satisfied concurrently (same 8 hours), whereas the crash warrant offers alternative time windows (12-month OR 36-month). Visual evidence: [Image 3] shows Sections 2B.13 and 2B.16 side by side, including the four-leg crash thresholds (five in 12 months / six in 36 months), the 300/200 units-per-hour criteria, and the provision that the volume thresholds may be reduced to 70 percent when the major-street 85th-percentile speed exceeds 40 mph. [Image 5] shows Section 2B.12, which lists both warrants (Warrant A: Crash Experience and Warrant D: 8-Hour Volume) among the all-way stop control warrants and states that satisfaction of a warrant does not in itself require installation. Citations: - Section 2B.13 Option §1 (p.79) - Section 2B.16 Option §1 (p.79) - Page 120 - Page 119
gold_answer: The crash warrant may apply with at least 5 correctable crashes in 12 months or 6 in 36 months. The volume warrant may apply when, for the same 8 hours, major-street entering volume is at least 300 units/hour and minor-street entering volume at least 200 units/hour, with a possible 70-percent adjustment if major-street 85th-percentile speed exceeds 40 mph.
